messages.content: What does a minimal TestItemRunner setup look like for a package?

Two pieces: a `test/runtests.jl` with one macro call, and `@testitem` blocks anywhere under the package.

```julia
# partial
# test/runtests.jl
using TestItemRunner
@run_package_tests
```

```julia
# partial
# test/parsing_tests.jl
@testitem "parse basics" begin
    @test parse(Int, "42") == 42
end
```

`TestItemRunner` exports exactly four macros: `@run_package_tests`, `@testitem`, `@testmodule`, `@testsnippet`. Each `@testitem` is discovered by parsing the source files, not by `include`, so there is no `include("parsing_tests.jl")` list to maintain. By default an item already has `using Test` and `using YourPackage` in scope, which is why `@test` works with no imports above.
My `@testitem` fails with `UndefVarError: helper not defined` even though another item defines `helper` as a global just above it. Why?

Each test item runs in its own fresh module, so nothing leaks between items, and there is no guaranteed order. A global defined in one item is invisible to the next.

```julia
# partial
@testitem "A" begin
    global counter = 1
end

@testitem "B" begin
    @test !@isdefined(counter)   # passes: B never sees A's globals
end
```

I ran this pair and B passes. Put shared code in a `@testsnippet` (spliced into each item that lists it) or a `@testmodule` (a module the item refers to by name), and list it with `setup=[...]`:

```julia
# partial
@testsnippet Data begin
    data = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
end

@testitem "sum" setup=[Data] begin
    @test sum(data) == 6.0
end
```

Because items are independent, you can run any single one with a filter and it behaves the same as in the full suite.
When should I use `@testmodule` and when `@testsnippet`?
Do I need `using Test` inside every `@testitem`?

No. By default each item starts with `using Test` and `using YourPackage` already evaluated, so `@test`, `@testset`, and your exports work directly. Extra packages still need an explicit `using` inside the item (and must be in the test environment).

```julia
# partial
@testitem "defaults" begin
    @test mysum([1, 2, 3]) == 6     # Test and the package are already imported
end
```

To opt out, pass `default_imports=false`. Then neither `@test` nor your package names are defined unless you import them yourself:

```julia
# partial
@testitem "bare" default_imports=false begin
    using Test
    @test 1 + 1 == 2
end
```

I checked that with `default_imports=false` an unqualified `@test` raises `UndefVarError`.
What does the `filter` argument of `@run_package_tests` receive, and how do I use it to skip slow items?

The filter is called once per test item with a named tuple that has exactly three fields: `filename`, `name`, and `tags`. Return `true` to run the item. Tag an item with `tags=[:slow]` and exclude it:

```julia
# partial
# test/runtests.jl
using TestItemRunner
@run_package_tests filter = ti -> !(:slow in ti.tags)
```

```julia
# partial
@testitem "big sweep" tags=[:slow] begin
    @test true
end
```

I verified the field names by printing `keys(ti)` inside the filter and confirmed the tagged item was absent from the summary. Tags are symbols; a plain `tags=[:slow]` literal is what the item parser recognizes.
I wrote `@run_package_tests filter = ti -> !(:slow in ti.tags), verbose = true` and got `syntax: invalid assignment location`. What is wrong?

The anonymous function body swallows the comma, so Julia parses `verbose = true` as part of the lambda. Give the filter a name, or separate the keyword arguments with spaces and no comma:

```julia
# partial
using TestItemRunner

keep(ti) = !(:slow in ti.tags)
@run_package_tests filter=keep verbose=true
```

The macro accepts only `filter`, `verbose`, `failfast`, and `testset`; any other keyword raises `Invalid argument`. I ran the named-function form and it works; the comma form with an inline lambda gave the syntax error above.
Is there a way to make the test run stop at the first failing item instead of running all 300 of them?

Pass `failfast=true`:

```julia
# partial
using TestItemRunner
@run_package_tests failfast=true
```

The run stops after the first item that fails or errors, and the remaining items are not run at all, so they appear in neither the summary nor the counts. I confirmed that the items after a deliberately failing one were missing from the summary. Use it for a quick red/green check; use a normal run when you need the complete list of failures.
How do I run only the test items whose names contain "sum" when running through `Pkg.test()`?

Put the condition in the `filter` in `test/runtests.jl`, matching on `ti.name`:

```julia
# partial
using TestItemRunner
@run_package_tests filter = ti -> occursin("sum", ti.name)
```

That is a temporary edit for a local run. For routine iteration, skip `Pkg.test()` entirely and use `julia_run_testitems` with `name_pattern="sum"` from the agent tool surface, which reuses warm worker processes and does not need `runtests.jl` edited. Keep the committed `runtests.jl` as the plain gate: `@run_package_tests`, plus at most a tag filter for items that should not run in CI.
Can I write `@testitem` blocks inside `src/`? What dependency would the package need?

Yes. The runner finds test items by parsing every `.jl` file under the package root, `src/` included. The `TestItems` package exists for this: its `@testitem`, `@testmodule`, and `@testsnippet` macros expand to `nothing`, so depending on it costs nothing at runtime.

```julia
# partial
# src/MyPkg.jl
module MyPkg
using TestItems
export double
double(x) = 2x

@testitem "double" begin
    @test double(2) == 4
end
end
```

I read the installed `TestItems` source to confirm the no-op macros. Most packages keep items under `test/`, which keeps the shipped source lean; in-source items are a choice for small, tightly coupled checks.
What is the difference between the `TestItems` and `TestItemRunner` packages?

`TestItems` only defines `@testitem`, `@testmodule`, and `@testsnippet` as macros that expand to `nothing`. It is a tiny dependency you can add to a package so items can live in `src/`. `TestItemRunner` provides `@run_package_tests`, which finds the items and runs them, and re-exports the same three macros. Put `TestItemRunner` in `test/Project.toml` and call it from `test/runtests.jl`. Editors and agent tooling (including the `julia_run_testitems` MCP tool) discover items by parsing source and run them in their own worker processes, so they do not need `runtests.jl` at all.
My teammate says `@testitem` blocks execute when the file is included. Correct?

No. The runner discovers items by parsing the source text; the files are not `include`d, and the macro itself does nothing when evaluated. Each item's body is evaluated later in its own fresh module only when the item is run. That is why you never list item files in `runtests.jl`, and why an item's body is not evaluated unless that item is selected to run.
I added a new test file under `test/` but `julia_list_testitems` does not show the items. What should I check?

Work through these in order:

1. Is the workspace set? All workspace tools fail until `julia_set_workspace_folders` has been called with the package root.
2. Does the file contain a literal `@testitem "name" begin ... end`? Items are detected syntactically. Write the name as a plain string literal.
3. Is the file under the folder you registered? Only `.jl` files below the workspace folders are scanned.
4. Is the call correct? Tags must be written as `tags=[:name]` with symbol literals; `setup=[Name]` must name setups that exist.

You do not need to re-register after editing: the workspace tracks the file system itself. If `julia_list_testitems` returns an empty list for the whole project, the project does not use TestItems at all, and you should fall back to its own test entrypoint (`Pkg.test()`).
Should an `@testitem` pull in shared helpers with `include("helpers.jl")`?
How do I make an item run only when an environment variable is set, e.g. for a slow integration check?

Tag the item and decide in `runtests.jl`, where the filter is ordinary Julia code:

```julia
# partial
# test/runtests.jl
using TestItemRunner

run_slow = get(ENV, "RUN_SLOW", "") == "1"
keep(ti) = run_slow || !(:slow in ti.tags)
@run_package_tests filter=keep
```

```julia
# partial
@testitem "integration" tags=[:slow] begin
    @test true
end
```

An item that is silently skipped by default can be forgotten, so print or document which tags are excluded by default and make CI set the variable.
Where do test-only dependencies go in a Julia package?

In `test/Project.toml`, never in the package's own `Project.toml`. Anything the tests use (`Test`, `TestItemRunner`, `OffsetArrays`, `BenchmarkTools`, ...) is listed under `[deps]` there:

```text
# test/Project.toml
[deps]
OffsetArrays = "6fe1bfb0-de20-5000-8ca7-80f57d26f881"
Test = "8dfed614-e22c-5e08-85e1-65c5234f0b40"
TestItemRunner = "f8b46487-2199-4994-9208-9a1283c18c0a"
```

`Pkg.test()` builds a temporary environment that merges the package with `test/Project.toml` and runs `test/runtests.jl` in it, so users of your package never download test dependencies. I ran this layout with `Pkg.test()`. Get UUIDs from the registry, not from memory (see the next lesson).
`Pkg.test()` fails with `expected package `Test [8dfed614]` to be registered`. My test/Project.toml lists `Test = "8dfed614-e22c-5e08-85e1-65c119b98c04"`.

The UUID is wrong. `Test` is a standard library, and the real UUID is `8dfed614-e22c-5e08-85e1-65c5234f0b40`. The first eight characters match, so the error message looks right, but Pkg cannot find any package with the full wrong UUID in the registry, which is what "to be registered" means here. I reproduced exactly this error with the wrong UUID and fixed it by correcting the line.

Never type UUIDs from memory. Let Pkg write them:

```text
julia --project=test -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.add("Test")'
```

If that creates `test/Manifest.toml`, delete it (see the lesson on test manifests); `test/Project.toml` is the file that matters.
`Pkg.test()` says `ArgumentError: Package Test not found in current path` although `using Test` works at the REPL.

`Test` is a standard library but still a dependency that must be declared for the test environment. At the REPL it is visible because the default environment stack includes the standard libraries, while `Pkg.test()` runs in the temporary test environment, which contains only what `Project.toml` and `test/Project.toml` declare. Add it to `test/Project.toml`:

```text
[deps]
Test = "8dfed614-e22c-5e08-85e1-65c5234f0b40"
```

I reproduced the error by omitting `Test` from `test/Project.toml` and the fix by adding it. The same applies to every package a test item imports with `using`.
Should I commit `test/Manifest.toml`?

No. The test environment is defined by `test/Project.toml` alone: `Pkg.test()` resolves a fresh temporary environment from it on every run, and the test-item tooling does the same in its own sandbox. A `test/Manifest.toml` left in place can interfere with how the test environment is resolved, and libraries conventionally do not commit manifests. Add `test/Manifest.toml` to `.gitignore`, delete one that appears, and do not run `Pkg.resolve()` or `Pkg.instantiate()` with `--project=test`, which would write it. Resolving the package's own project (`--project=.`) is fine because it does not touch `test/`.
I want to iterate on one failing test. Can I add my package as a dev dependency inside `test/` so I can run `julia --project=test`?

Don't. Running `Pkg.develop(path=".")` inside `test/` writes the package into `test/Project.toml` and creates a `test/Manifest.toml`, and the package then ends up as a dependency of its own tests. `Pkg.test()` builds its own merged environment per run and ignores those edits, so you get a file that looks authoritative but is not what the gate runs.

For fast iteration use the warm test tooling instead: `julia_set_workspace_folders` on the package root, then `julia_run_testitems` with `name_pattern` and `max_workers=1`. It activates the test environment for you and keeps compiled state between runs. Keep `Pkg.test()` for the gate.
Why does `Pkg.test()` take so long after a one-line edit, even though I just ran my code in the REPL?

`Pkg.test()` starts a new Julia process and, since Julia 1.10 up to 1.12, passes `--check-bounds=yes` to it. Julia keys the precompile cache on flags like that, so the package is precompiled a second time, independently of the cache your normal `using MyPkg` uses. Once both caches exist, each source change costs a recompile in each mode that you actually run.

I verified the flag by printing `Base.JLOptions().check_bounds` inside `test/runtests.jl`: it printed `1` on 1.10 and 1.12. On 1.13.2 the same test printed `0`, because the 1.13 `Pkg.test` docs say it inherits the current session's setting instead of forcing `yes`. So the double compile is a property of Julia 1.10-1.12; check your version before assuming it.
How do I check which `--check-bounds` mode my tests are running under?

Print `Base.JLOptions().check_bounds` from inside the tests: `0` is the default, `1` is `--check-bounds=yes`, and `2` is `--check-bounds=no`.

```julia
println("check_bounds = ", Base.JLOptions().check_bounds)
```

In a default session this prints `check_bounds = 0`. Put the line at the top of `test/runtests.jl` once to see what `Pkg.test()` gives you on each Julia version you support. I measured `1` for `Pkg.test()` on 1.10 and 1.12, and `0` on 1.13.2.
Why should the pre-merge test gate run with `--check-bounds=yes`?

`--check-bounds=yes` makes every `@inbounds` annotation inert, so an out-of-range index in code marked `@inbounds` raises `BoundsError` instead of silently reading or writing arbitrary memory. The gate is the one place where an unjustified `@inbounds` has to show up as a failure. In my run, a function with `@inbounds v[1]` on an empty vector raised `BoundsError` under `check_bounds = 1` and returned a value without any error under `check_bounds = 0`, so a test using `@test_throws BoundsError` passed in one mode and failed in the other.

Practical consequence: if a package uses `@inbounds`, its tests need to run at least once under `--check-bounds=yes`, either through plain `Pkg.test()` on Julia 1.10-1.12 (which force it) or, on 1.13 and later (where `Pkg.test()` inherits the session's setting), by passing `julia_args=["--check-bounds=yes"]` explicitly. In CI, `julia-actions/julia-runtest` takes `check_bounds: 'yes'`; state it explicitly rather than relying on its default.
Can I make `Pkg.test()` reuse my normal precompile cache?

Yes, by overriding the flag with `julia_args`, which Pkg appends after its own flags so the last one wins:

```julia
# partial
using Pkg
Pkg.test(; julia_args=["--check-bounds=auto"])
```

This matters on Julia 1.10-1.12, where Pkg forces `--check-bounds=yes`; I confirmed on 1.10 and 1.12 that the test process then reports `Base.JLOptions().check_bounds == 0` instead of `1`. On 1.13 the default is already `0` unless the session was started with the flag, so the override changes nothing. Use this to iterate on a failing test. Do not make it the default or put it in CI: it also switches off the bounds-check safety net described above, so an out-of-bounds bug in `@inbounds` code can pass. Run the real gate with Pkg's default.
I put `Pkg.test(; julia_args=["--check-bounds=auto"])` in our CI script to speed it up. Review that.

Remove it. On Julia 1.10-1.12 the speedup comes from skipping the second precompile that Pkg's forced `--check-bounds=yes` causes (on 1.13 the override does nothing, since Pkg no longer forces the flag), and the price is that every `@inbounds` in the package becomes active during the tests. Any out-of-range access in such code then reads or writes memory silently and the test can still pass.

CI is the safety net, so on 1.10-1.12 it should run with Pkg's default (`--check-bounds=yes`), and on 1.13 and later it should pass `julia_args=["--check-bounds=yes"]` explicitly, because the default there inherits the session setting. If CI time is the problem, split the suite across jobs by tag instead.
On Julia 1.13 I assumed `Pkg.test()` always runs with bounds checks forced on. Is that right?

Not on 1.13. In 1.10 through 1.12 Pkg hardcodes `--check-bounds=yes` for the test subprocess. In the 1.13.2 `Pkg` source that flag is gone from the subprocess flags, and the docs say tests run "with the same `check-bounds` setting as the current Julia session". I confirmed it: `Pkg.test()` printed `check_bounds = 0` for a package whose `@inbounds` function did not raise, and started `julia --check-bounds=yes` made it print `1`.

If you rely on bounds checks being on during tests, ask for them explicitly:

```julia
# partial
using Pkg
Pkg.test(; julia_args=["--check-bounds=yes"])
```

This works on every version and states the intent in the command.
How often should I run the full test suite while developing?

Rarely. During iteration run only the test items related to the change (a name pattern, a tag, or one file). Run the full suite as a gate at two points: before a commit or merge that touches shared core code, whose blast radius reaches beyond one component, and as the final check before merging. A change confined to one component's files is covered by that component's items.

With the agent tools, the iteration step is `julia_run_testitems` with `name_pattern` (or `items`) and `max_workers=1`; the gate is a cold `Pkg.test()` from the package root. The cold run is what catches stale-definition problems that a long-lived warm process can hide.
I changed the planner that every algorithm in my package routes through. Which tests do I run?

This is a shared-core change, so it needs the full suite as a pre-commit gate, in addition to the items for the planner itself. Iterate first with the planner's own items (`julia_run_testitems` with a `name_pattern` or `file_pattern`, `max_workers=1`), then run everything once cold with `Pkg.test()` before committing.

The rule of thumb: the filtered run is enough when a change cannot affect other components; the full run is for changes whose blast radius you cannot bound to one component. When in doubt, name the specific risk ("other algorithms inherit this planner") and run the items that cover it.
I edited `src/solver.jl` and the test still shows the old result. What should I do?

First suspect stale code, not a wrong test. In order:

1. Run the item again with `julia_run_testitems` (use `name_pattern` and `max_workers=1`). Test workers hot-reload source edits through Revise before running.
2. If the edit was to a `struct` definition or something Revise cannot apply, call `julia_list_test_processes` and then `julia_terminate_test_process` for the idle worker; the next run starts a fresh one.
3. If the result is still impossible, run the real gate once with a cold `Pkg.test()` from the package root. A cold process has no Revise state, so it shows what the code on disk really does.

A result that contradicts the source you just edited is a staleness symptom until proven otherwise. Do not keep editing code to chase it.
What is the difference between `julia_run_testitems` and `Pkg.test()` for an agent?

`julia_run_testitems` runs items in worker processes that stay alive between calls and pick up edits through Revise, reports per-item results, and activates the test environment for you. `Pkg.test()` starts a new process every time, compiles the package again (and, on 1.10-1.12, again under `--check-bounds=yes`), and prints one long log.

Use `julia_run_testitems` for the inner loop and `Pkg.test()` for the final gate. If `julia_list_testitems` returns nothing, the project does not use TestItems and `Pkg.test()` is the only runner.
Our CI tests on Julia 1.10 and the current release. I ran everything locally and it passed. Can I call it green?

Only for the version you ran. Without a `julia_cmd`, `julia_run_testitems` uses the default juliaup channel, so a green local run says nothing about the other entry in the matrix. Version differences are real: for example, `Pkg.test()` forces `--check-bounds=yes` on 1.10-1.12 but inherits the session setting on 1.13, and inference and compiler-trimming results change between releases.

Read the matrix from `.github/workflows/*.yml`, then run the suite once per entry, passing `julia_cmd` set to that version's `julia` executable, and report which version each result came from. A bare "N passed" is not a gate.
How do I run the same test items on the LTS and on the release from the agent tools?

Call `julia_run_testitems` once per version and pass `julia_cmd` set to the path of that version's `julia` binary (juliaup installs them as `julia-<version>/bin/julia` under its `juliaup` directory; `juliaup status` lists the versions). Keep `max_workers=1` or a small number on each call.

```text
julia_run_testitems  name_pattern="parse"  max_workers=1  julia_cmd=<path to julia 1.10 binary>
julia_run_testitems  name_pattern="parse"  max_workers=1  julia_cmd=<path to julia 1.13 binary>
```

For an interactive session on a specific version, `julia_create_session` takes the same `julia_cmd` parameter. Report each result with its version.
Do I need a second, older Julia installed just to test on the LTS?

To claim LTS compatibility, yes: `[compat] julia = "1.10"` is only a promise until a 1.10 run passes. Install it with `juliaup add 1.10` and run the tests with it. In a shell, `julia +1.10 --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.test()'` selects that channel; from the agent tools pass `julia_cmd`. A 1.10 run also surfaces things a new release hides, such as the Manifest warning about a manifest resolved with a different Julia version, or code relying on features newer than the LTS.
Is it wasteful to test on both the LTS and the release for a small change?

For iteration, yes: use one version and a filtered run. For the final gate, no. Behavior that differs between versions is not hypothetical: the number printed by `Base.JLOptions().check_bounds` under `Pkg.test()` is 1 on 1.10 and 1.12 but 0 on 1.13.2, and the same suite passing on the release while failing on another version is a routine outcome of compiler and standard-library changes. The gate should cover every version in the CI matrix.
What goes into `[compat]` for the test dependencies?

Bound each dependency listed in the package's own `Project.toml`. For `test/Project.toml`, bound the non-stdlib packages too (for example `OffsetArrays = "1"`), choosing lower bounds that work on the LTS. After editing any `Project.toml`, run `Pkg.resolve()` for the package's own project; resolver errors point to conflicts that you would otherwise hit later in CI. Do not create or commit a `test/Manifest.toml` to pin versions.
My package needs `OffsetArrays` only in tests. I ran `] add OffsetArrays` in the package project. Is that right?

No, that makes it a runtime dependency of every user. Add it to the test environment instead:

```text
julia --project=test -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.add("OffsetArrays")'
```

Then remove `test/Manifest.toml` if it was created, and move the line out of the package's `Project.toml` (`[deps]` and `[compat]`) if you already added it there. A stray `--project=.` run from the wrong directory is the usual cause of a test dependency ending up in the package's own project.
A teammate says `Pkg.test()` is the same as running `include("test/runtests.jl")` in my REPL. Correct?

No. `Pkg.test()` creates a temporary environment merging the package and `test/Project.toml`, then runs `test/runtests.jl` in a fresh process with its own flags (`--check-bounds=yes` on 1.10-1.12, no startup file by default, depwarn and inline settings taken from the parent). `include("test/runtests.jl")` runs in your current session with whatever packages and definitions are already loaded, so it can pass because of REPL state that a clean run lacks, and it fails if the test dependencies are not in your active environment.
How do I pass an argument to `test/runtests.jl` when using `Pkg.test`?

Use the `test_args` keyword, which becomes `ARGS` inside `runtests.jl`:

```julia
# partial
using Pkg
Pkg.test(; test_args=["fast"])
```

```julia
# partial
# test/runtests.jl
using TestItemRunner
only_fast = "fast" in ARGS
@run_package_tests filter = ti -> !only_fast || :fast in ti.tags
```

The `test_args` and `julia_args` keywords both appear in the `Pkg.test` method signature in 1.13.2. For ordinary iteration the agent test tools make this unnecessary, because `tags` and `name_pattern` are tool parameters.
Does the `filter` I put in `test/runtests.jl` apply when I run tests through `julia_run_testitems`?

No. The tool discovers and runs items itself; it does not execute `runtests.jl`. In my check an item tagged `:slow` that `runtests.jl` excluded still ran through the tool. Express the same selection with the tool's own parameters: `tags`, `name_pattern`, `file_pattern`, `package`, or explicit `items` ids from `julia_list_testitems`. Keep `runtests.jl` for the `Pkg.test()` gate and for CI.
Is there an easy way to see which items took the longest so I can tag them `:slow`?

Run once with `julia_run_testitems` and `include_passing=true`: the per-item list reports each item's duration in milliseconds. In the summary, the duration is wall-clock time for the whole run, not the sum of the items (items run in parallel, so the sum overshoots). Tag the long ones, then use `tags` to include or exclude them. The first run in a fresh worker includes compilation, so rerun before you decide an item is slow.
Should test dependencies like `BenchmarkTools` go in the package's compat section?

Only if the package itself imports them. Benchmarks and test helpers belong in `test/Project.toml` (or a separate `benchmark/Project.toml`). A package that lists `BenchmarkTools` in its own `[deps]` forces it on every user, and its install and load cost lands on all of them.
Why did all my test items error immediately after I changed `test/Project.toml`, with none of them reporting a failed assertion?

When every item errors in seconds and none shows a failed `@test`, the test environment failed to activate, not the code. Fetch the detail for one id with `julia_get_testitem_detail`: the message names the cause. I reproduced it with a wrong `Test` UUID: every item reported `Environment activation failed for package 'MyPkg': expected package `Test [8dfed614]` to be registered`. Fix `test/Project.toml` (correct UUIDs, no misspelled package names) and rerun. If the whole worker died before running anything, read the `testprocess://{process_id}/output` resource for the precompile error.
Walk me through running one test item with the Julia MCP tools after I edit its code.

1. `julia_set_workspace_folders` with the package root (once per workspace; it must precede every other workspace tool, and later edits are picked up automatically).
2. `julia_list_testitems` with `name_pattern` to get the item's id, which looks like `MyPkg@a1b2c3d4/test/parsing_tests.jl::parse basics`.
3. `julia_run_testitems` with `items=[<id>]` and `max_workers=1`.
4. If it failed, `julia_get_testitem_detail` with the `testrun_id` and the failing ids for the message, stack trace, and output.
5. Edit the code, then `julia_rerun_failed` with that `testrun_id`; the worker reloads the edit through Revise.

The run result deliberately lists only per-item statuses; messages and output come from `julia_get_testitem_detail`.
Do I need to call anything after editing a test file so the tools see my changes?

No. `julia_set_workspace_folders` makes the workspace track the file system itself, so new, renamed, or edited `@testitem` blocks show up in `julia_list_testitems` on their own (the scan interval is one second by default). Call `julia_set_workspace_folders` again only to change which folders are loaded; calling it replaces the previous configuration.
What number should I pass for `max_workers` and why is it needed at all?

Always pass it. Without it the default is the number of CPU threads, capped at 8 and at one worker per 3 GiB of system memory, and each worker is a full Julia process that loads your package and its test environment. For a heavy package that is many gigabytes.

- one item, or a few you are iterating on: `max_workers=1`
- the full suite when wall-clock time matters: 2 to 4, leaving cores free for other work

The parameter limits concurrency within one run; it does not limit how many idle workers are kept afterward (see the lesson on worker pools).
I ran `julia_run_testitems` three times with `max_workers=2` and now my machine is swapping. I thought `max_workers` capped the processes.

It caps parallelism inside one run, not the total number of worker processes. When a run ends, its workers are returned to a pool and kept alive for the next run (that is how repeat runs skip startup), and successive runs can add to the pool. Each idle worker still holds the memory of your loaded package.

Reap them:

1. `julia_list_test_processes` to see the workers.
2. `julia_terminate_test_process` with each `process_id` you no longer need.

Do this after the last run of a task, and before benchmarks, which machine state would otherwise distort. A terminated worker pays full startup and precompilation on the next run, so terminate between tasks, not between iterations.
A test run seems stuck. Can I just `kill -9` the Julia worker processes?

Not while the run is live. Killing a worker out from under a running test run strands it: the run never completes, so its worker pool is never cleaned up, and the leftover processes keep holding memory and can make unrelated runs look hung.

Correct order:

1. `julia_cancel_testrun` with the `testrun_id`. Unfinished items are abandoned and their workers are killed.
2. `julia_list_test_processes` for anything left, then `julia_terminate_test_process` per id.
3. Only if processes survive both, kill by explicit PID from the shell, never with `pkill -f julia`, which can match and kill your own shell.
What is the difference between `timeout` and `max_wait_seconds` in `julia_run_testitems`?

They are independent limits on different things.

- `timeout` is per test item, in seconds. An item still running when it expires is reported as errored with a message reading "timed out after N seconds", its worker is killed and replaced, and the rest of the run continues.
- `max_wait_seconds` limits only how long this tool call blocks (default 600). If the run is still going, the call returns `status: "running"` with partial results and a `testrun_id`; the run is not stopped.

Set `timeout` when a hanging item must not block the suite. Set `max_wait_seconds` to match your client's tool-call limit. I confirmed both: an item that slept 30 seconds was errored at `timeout=8`, and with `max_wait_seconds=2` the call returned with status "running" while the item was still pending.
`julia_run_testitems` returned `status: "running"`. Did my tests fail?

No, it means the call stopped waiting, not that the run stopped. The run continues in the background. Do this:

1. Call `julia_get_testrun_results` with the `testrun_id`. It returns immediately; repeat with some time between calls until `status` is no longer `"running"`.
2. Do not start a second run of the same items while the first is still going.
3. If it is a hang rather than a slow suite, `julia_cancel_testrun`, then rerun with a per-item `timeout` so the stuck item is errored and the others complete.

Raising `max_wait_seconds` costs nothing for fast suites, since the call returns as soon as the run finishes.
One item deadlocks (a blocking `take!`), and `julia_run_testitems` never returns. What do I do?

It will not return by itself, and it cannot hang the call forever either: after `max_wait_seconds` (default 600) the call returns `status: "running"` with a `testrun_id`. A hanging item never finishes on its own, so:

```text
julia_cancel_testrun    testrun_id=<id>
julia_run_testitems     items=[<ids>]  max_workers=1  timeout=60
```

With `timeout` set, the deadlocked item is errored with "timed out after 60 seconds", its worker is killed and replaced, and the rest of the suite completes. Then fix the item; for example, give the `take!` a timeout path so a failure is reported instead of a hang.
The detail for a timed-out item printed a huge wall of text. How do I get something readable?

A timed-out item's output includes a task dump and profile written by the worker's watchdog; the one I inspected was over 100 KB. The tool keeps only the tail by default (8000 bytes). Ask for less with `max_output_bytes` and `max_stack_frames` on `julia_get_testitem_detail`, and read the `messages` field first: it holds the one-line cause ("Test item 'slow one' timed out after 8.0 seconds"). The full stream stays available through the output resource that the detail result names, if you really need it.
How do I get the failure message for several failed items without making many calls?

Pass all ids at once. `julia_get_testitem_detail` takes `testitem_ids` (a list) together with the `testrun_id`, so one call covers every item you care about. Unknown ids are reported per item instead of failing the call. Use `max_messages`, `max_stack_frames`, and `max_output_bytes` to bound the size.

```text
julia_get_testitem_detail  testrun_id=<id>  testitem_ids=[<id1>, <id2>, <id3>]  max_stack_frames=5
```
After a full run with 3 failures, how do I rerun just those?

Use `julia_rerun_failed` with the earlier run's `testrun_id`. It reruns only the failed and errored items, reuses that run's settings (override with `julia_cmd`, `julia_args`, `max_workers`, `timeout`, or `max_wait_seconds` if needed), and returns a new `testrun_id` while leaving the original intact. The usual loop is: run, read detail, edit, `julia_rerun_failed`, repeat. Pass `max_workers` again on the rerun if you want a different cap from the original run.
Are test item ids stable across edits? I want to keep a list of failing ids while I fix them.

Yes. The id depends only on the package, file path, and item name, in the form `MyPkg@a1b2c3d4/test/parsing_tests.jl::parse basics`. It stays valid across edits to the body, so you can keep the list and pass it to `julia_run_testitems` through `items`. Renaming the item or moving the file changes the id.
How do I run every item with a given tag, and how do I see the tags first?

`julia_list_testitems` returns each item's `tags`, and both it and `julia_run_testitems` accept `tags` as a filter that keeps items carrying at least one of the listed tags. The other filters are `name_pattern` (regex on item names), `file_pattern` (regex on file URIs), `package`, and `items` (explicit ids).

```text
julia_list_testitems   tags=["fast"]
julia_run_testitems    tags=["fast"]  max_workers=1
```

Filters combine, so `tags=["fast"]` with a `file_pattern` narrows to fast items in matching files.
The first `julia_run_testitems` call of the session took far longer than the next ones, and everything errored. Is the package broken?

Not necessarily. The first call starts workers, activates the test environment, precompiles, and loads your package; later calls reuse warm workers. If all items errored within seconds of starting and none reports a failed `@test`, call `julia_get_testitem_detail` on one id: an environment activation error (for example a bad UUID in `test/Project.toml`) appears in its message. If a worker died before any item ran, the cause is in the `testprocess://{process_id}/output` resource. Precompile slow dependencies once up front with `Pkg.precompile()` in a foreground command, then run the tests.
How do I get line coverage for my tests with the Julia MCP tools?

Run with `mode="Coverage"` and then read the result with `julia_get_coverage_results`:

```text
julia_run_testitems         mode="Coverage"  max_workers=1
julia_get_coverage_results
```

Coverage collection applies to the packages under test. Coverage-mode runs use their own worker processes that are retired afterward instead of pooled, so they are not kept in the pool for later runs.
One worker's memory keeps growing over a long suite. Any control?

`julia_run_testitems` takes `memory_threshold`, a fraction of total system memory. After each item, a worker whose resident memory exceeds it is recycled, and its remaining items go to other workers, so no results are lost. It is off by default. Remember that the fraction is of total memory, so on a large machine even a worker worth recycling is a small fraction (for example 0.05). Combine it with `max_workers` rather than replacing it.
I need syntax and lint feedback on a test file I just edited, without running it. Which tool?

`julia_get_diagnostics`. It parses and lints without compiling or running anything, so it is cheaper than any evaluation. It needs `julia_set_workspace_folders` first. Checks that depend on the environment, such as unresolved imports, need `wait_for_ready: true`. Use it to answer "does this parse" after an edit, then run the item with `julia_run_testitems`.
Can I use `julia_eval_code` to run a single test body quickly?

Yes, for exploration. Create a session with `julia_create_session` (pass `project` and `package`, and `use_test_env=true` if you need the test dependencies), load the package, and evaluate the body. Variables and compiled code persist, and Revise applies source edits on each call. But the item itself runs differently: in its own fresh module with the default imports and setups. Before you trust a pass, run the real item through `julia_run_testitems` once, so it passes in the same isolation CI uses.
Should I kill and recreate my Julia session to get a clean test run?

No. Killing the session discards all compiled code, so the next call recompiles everything, and there is no restart tool. Revise recompiles only what changed. Recreate a session only when you change the `include` graph or hit a stale-definition error, and then pass the environment that `julia_list_sessions` reported to `julia_create_session`. For a clean-state check, use the cold `Pkg.test()` gate instead, which starts a fresh process by design.
My agent edits `struct Foo` and the test worker keeps failing with a method error from the old definition. What now?

A struct redefinition is the kind of change Revise sometimes cannot apply inside a long-lived process. Terminate the affected worker with `julia_terminate_test_process` (find its id with `julia_list_test_processes`); it loses its compiled state, so the next run pays full startup, but it loads the new definition. Do this only when needed. Ordinary method-body edits are picked up by Revise without it.
Is it safe to run `julia_run_testitems` for the same package from two agent sessions at once?

Every run adds workers to the pool, and every worker is a full Julia process holding your package in memory, so several sessions with a large `max_workers` can exhaust RAM. Keep `max_workers` small (1 to 2) on each, and reap idle workers when finished. If `julia_create_session` starts failing with "has died" on every attempt, suspect memory pressure and free workers first before assuming the server is broken.
Give me the exact order of calls to gate a commit with the Julia MCP tools.

```text
1. julia_set_workspace_folders  folders=[<package root>]
2. julia_run_testitems          max_workers=2  timeout=300      # full suite on the default Julia
3. julia_get_testitem_detail    testrun_id=<id>  testitem_ids=[<failed ids>]   # only if something failed
4. julia_run_testitems          max_workers=2  julia_cmd=<other CI version's julia>
5. julia_list_test_processes, then julia_terminate_test_process per id        # reap workers
6. cold Pkg.test() from the package root                                   # final gate
```

Steps 2 and 4 cover each version in the CI matrix; step 6 catches stale-definition and test-environment problems that warm workers can hide. Report which version each result came from.
My agent summary says "all tests pass" but it only ran the items matching `name_pattern="parse"`. Is that a fair report?

No. A filtered run proves only that the selected items passed. State the scope in the report ("12 of 140 items, matching 'parse', Julia 1.13") and run the full suite before calling a shared-core change verified. A pass count without its scope reads as a claim about the whole tree.
Why do the tools report durations in milliseconds in one place and seconds in another?

Inputs and outputs use different units: `timeout` and `max_wait_seconds` are in seconds, while every duration in a result is in milliseconds (per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run). Convert before comparing a `timeout=8` setting against a result showing `duration: 8321`.
I want the output of a passing item. `julia_run_testitems` shows nothing for passing items.

Passing items are omitted from the list by default and only counted in the summary. Set `include_passing=true` to list them, then use `julia_get_testitem_detail` for the captured stdout/stderr of the item you care about. Failed and errored items are listed first, and `max_items` (default 200) caps the list.
A colleague wants to know which tool to use to see whether a worker died during precompilation.

`julia_list_test_processes` shows the workers and their status, and the process output resource `testprocess://{process_id}/output` holds its raw output, where precompilation and startup failures appear. Per-item detail will not show it when the worker died before running any item.
My new `@testitem` does not appear in `julia_list_testitems`, and the file parses fine. What else could it be?

Item declarations are validated separately from Julia syntax. An item with an option the parser does not recognize is dropped from the list. Call `julia_get_diagnostics` with `path` set to the file; item problems come back with source `Testitem`. I reproduced it with `@testitem "has retries" retries=2 begin ... end`: the item was missing from the list and the diagnostic read `Unknown keyword argument.`

The recognized options are `tags` (a vector of symbol literals), `setup` (a vector of setup names), `default_imports` (a Bool literal), and `skip`. The final argument must be a `begin ... end` block and all other arguments must be `key=value`.
How do I conditionally skip a test item, for example on Windows?

Use the `skip` option with an expression. A skipped item is reported with status `skipped` and is not run:

```julia
# partial
@testitem "needs a POSIX shell" skip=Sys.iswindows() begin
    @test success(`true`)
end
```

I confirmed that `skip=true` produces a `skipped` item in the run summary and that `skip=(VERSION < v"1.0")` (false) runs normally. Use `skip` for platform or version conditions; use tags for "usually excluded" categories like slow items.
We are moving from ReTestItems.jl to TestItemRunner.jl. What changes in the tests?

`@testitem` bodies mostly stay the same. What changes:

```julia
# partial
# test/runtests.jl, before
using ReTestItems, MyPkg
runtests(MyPkg)

# after
using TestItemRunner
@run_package_tests
```

1. `test/Project.toml`: replace `ReTestItems` with `TestItemRunner`.
2. Item options: the TestItemRunner parser accepts `tags`, `setup`, `default_imports`, and `skip`. Any other keyword makes the item invisible with "Unknown keyword argument" (check with `julia_get_diagnostics`), so review every ReTestItems-specific option.
3. Selection: ReTestItems' `name`/`tags` arguments to `runtests` become a `filter` function receiving `(; filename, name, tags)` in `@run_package_tests`.
4. Setups: use `@testsnippet` and `@testmodule` with `setup=[...]`.

The agent tools (`julia_list_testitems`, `julia_run_testitems`, `julia_rerun_failed`) drive TestItemRunner-style items directly.
We have five packages in a monorepo, all on ReTestItems, and I want them all on TestItemRunner. Where should I start?

With the smallest or newest package, not all five. Migrate one, run its suite on every CI Julia version, and let the owner look at the diff before touching the rest. A big-bang migration across thousands of existing tests is hard to review and hard to revert if the pattern needs adjusting. A broad "yes, migrate everything" answer is provisional until someone has seen the first concrete diff. New packages start on TestItemRunner immediately; existing ones follow one at a time, each as its own change.
Migrating one package: my ReTestItems suite had `retries` on flaky items. What do I do on TestItemRunner?

TestItemRunner's item parser does not accept `retries`; the item would be dropped with "Unknown keyword argument". Remove the option rather than leaving it, and treat each former flaky item as a bug to fix: find the nondeterminism (shared global state, timing, unseeded RNG, filesystem races) and make the test deterministic. If an item cannot be fixed soon, mark it `skip=true` with a comment naming the reason, so the suite stays honest rather than retrying until it passes.
Is it worth writing tests as plain `@testset` files with `include` instead of test items?

For a small package, `@testset` plus `include` works. Test items earn their keep as the suite grows: each item is self-contained, so you can run any one alone, in parallel workers, or re-run just the failures; failures are reported per item; and tooling can list and select items without executing the file. Plain `include`d scripts share one module and run top to bottom, so an item that passes only because an earlier one defined a variable is invisible until someone runs it alone. Choose items when you want filtered iteration to be a normal workflow.
Show me how to test that an error message is helpful, not just that an error occurs.

Review this test.

```julia
using Test
parse_port(s) = (p = tryparse(Int, s); p === nothing ? error("bad port") : p)
@test_throws ErrorException parse_port("abc")
```

It passes for any `error(...)` call in `parse_port`, including a bug unrelated to port parsing, such as an undefined helper function that happens to throw a different `ErrorException`. Assert the message, which is the part users read:

```julia
using Test
parse_port(s) = (p = tryparse(Int, s); p === nothing ? throw(ArgumentError("bad port: $s")) : p)
@test_throws ArgumentError parse_port("abc")
@test_throws "bad port" parse_port("abc")
```

The function throws `ArgumentError` for bad input, and the test checks both the type and the message; the message match is the more informative one.
Is `@test_throws ErrorException ...` ever enough?

Yes, when the contract is only "throws this type" and the message is deliberately unspecified, or when it embeds details you do not want to freeze (addresses, timestamps). In every other case also check the message, because the message is what a user sees. Both can be tested in separate lines: one for the type, one for the string.
My function is declared for `AbstractVector`. How should I test that it really is generic?

Fix this function so it is correct for arrays with arbitrary axes.

```julia
function total(A::AbstractVector)
    s = zero(eltype(A))
    for i in 1:length(A)
        s += A[i]
    end
    return s
end
```

It indexes `1:length(A)`, which is only valid when the axes start at 1. On `OffsetArray(collect(1:3), -2:0)` it raises `BoundsError: attempt to access 3-element OffsetArray(::Vector{Int64}, -2:0) ... at index [1]` (I ran this). Iterate the array's own indices:

```julia
function total(A::AbstractVector)
    s = zero(eltype(A))
    for i in eachindex(A)
        s += A[i]
    end
    return s
end

@assert total([1, 2, 3]) == 6
@assert total(view(collect(1:10), 2:4)) == 9
```

Then add a test with an offset input so the bug cannot return:

```julia
# partial
using OffsetArrays, Test
@test total(OffsetArray([1, 2, 3], -2:0)) == 6
```

If you really want 1-based code, say so with `Base.require_one_based_indexing(A)` at the top: callers with an `OffsetArray` then get an immediate error ("offset arrays are not supported but got an array with index other than 1") rather than a wrong result.

It iterates `eachindex(A)` (offset indices like `-2:0`) but writes into a plain `Vector`, whose indices start at 1. I ran it on `OffsetArray([1,2,3], -2:0)`: `BoundsError: attempt to access 3-element Vector{Int64} at index [-2]`. Allocate the output so it inherits the input's axes:

```julia
copy_vec(A::AbstractVector) = (out = similar(A); for i in eachindex(A); out[i] = A[i]; end; out)

@assert copy_vec([1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3]
@assert axes(copy_vec(view(collect(1:9), 3:5))) == (Base.OneTo(3),)
```

With an `OffsetArray` input the result has axes `-2:0` as well, which is the property to assert in a test: `@test axes(copy_vec(A)) == axes(A)`.
Which wrapped array types should I put in a generic-code test?

A small fixed set that covers the failure classes:

1. A plain `Array` (baseline).
2. An `OffsetArray` with a non-1 first index (breaks `1:length` and `1:n` loops).
3. A `view` of a larger array (breaks code that assumes contiguous parent storage, and it checks that results do not alias the parent unexpectedly).
4. A strided view such as `view(v, 1:2:end)` when the function should work on it.
5. Where relevant, a `PermutedDimsArray` or `reshape` for matrices.

Loop over the set with the same assertions: `@test f(B) == f(collect(B))` and `@test axes(g(B)) == axes(B)`. A function whose annotation says `AbstractArray` earns those tests; if you will not support them, narrow the annotation instead.
What should a generic test assert about the output's axes?

By the indexing axiom, `a = b[idxs]` satisfies `a[j] === b[idxs[j]]`, so the result takes its values from `b` and its axes from the indices. For a function that maps an input to an index-matched output, assert `axes(result) == axes(input)`. For a function that selects with some index set, assert `axes(result) == axes(idxs)`. These checks catch code that builds output with `Vector{T}(undef, length(x))` and silently drops the input's axes.
Add a regression test for this fix: `eachindex` replaced `1:length` in `running_total`. What do I write?
Is a passing test suite proof that my comparison helper is correct?

No. A comparison helper (golden-file diff, tree equality) can have a branch that never runs, so the suite stays green on any input. Check what each predicate that gates a content check means for a concrete leaf case, and make the helper fail on a deliberately corrupted input:

```julia
struct Node
    tag::String
    text::String
    kids::Vector{Node}
end

# Intended: "has element children". Actual: also true for a text-only leaf.
has_children(n::Node) = !isempty(n.kids) || !isempty(n.text)

function same(a::Node, b::Node)
    a.tag == b.tag || return false
    if has_children(a)
        length(a.kids) == length(b.kids) || return false
        return all(same(x, y) for (x, y) in zip(a.kids, b.kids))
    end
    return a.text == b.text
end

a = Node("choice", "aaaa", Node[])
b = Node("choice", "bbbb", Node[])
same(a, b)   # → true: the text of a leaf is never compared
```

Fix the predicate and prove the helper can fail:

```julia
# partial
using Test
has_children(n::Node) = !isempty(n.kids)
@test !same(a, b)
@test same(a, Node("choice", "aaaa", Node[]))
```

Always include a negative control: feed the helper two inputs that must differ.
Our XML round-trip test has been green for years, and now a backend swap makes it fail. Is the new backend wrong?

Possibly not. A test comparison utility whose gating predicate is looser than intended can hide real differences for as long as the test exists, including on the original backend. When a swap changes what "children" or "leaf" means, the stricter predicate can expose a bug that was always there. Check the old backend with the corrected comparison before blaming the new one: if the old code also fails, the helper was masking the bug. Then add a negative-control test (inputs that must compare unequal) so the helper cannot go quiet again.
How do I test that my function is type stable?

Use `@inferred` inside a test. It throws if the inferred return type differs from the type of the value actually returned.

```julia
using Test

stable(x) = x > 0 ? 1 : 2
unstable(x) = x > 0 ? 1 : 1.0

@test (@inferred stable(1)) == 1
msg = try
    @inferred unstable(1)
catch err
    sprint(showerror, err)
end
println(msg)
```

The failing call prints `return type Int64 does not match inferred return type Union{Float64, Int64}`. Test with each concrete input type you support (`Float32`, `Float64`, an `OffsetArray`), not just one.
How do I compare floating point results in tests?

Use `isapprox` (`≈`) with a tolerance chosen for the algorithm. Exact `==` on computed floats is a latent failure.

```julia
using Test
@test 0.1 + 0.2 ≈ 0.3
println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)   # false
@test isapprox(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3; atol=1e-12)
```

`≈` uses a relative tolerance by default, which is useless near zero: comparing against `0.0` needs an explicit `atol`. Use `==` only where exactness is the contract (integers, a bit-exact reference).
How do I test that a warning is emitted?

`@test_logs` checks the log records an expression produces:

```julia
using Test
r = @test_logs (:warn, "careful") @warn "careful"
```

Pass `(level, message)` patterns in the order the records are emitted; the test fails if the records differ or extra records appear (unless you use `match_mode=:any`). It keeps warning-producing code from emitting noise in the test log.
What does `@test_broken` do and when should I use it?

`@test_broken expr` records a known failure: while `expr` is false or throws, it counts as "broken" and the suite stays green; when `expr` starts passing it is reported as an error, which forces you to convert it into a normal `@test`. Use it for a bug you have decided not to fix yet, with an issue link in a comment. Do not use it to silence a flaky test; a skipped item with a stated reason is more honest.

```julia
using Test
@test_broken 1 == 2
```
What is a sensible layout for the test directory with TestItemRunner?

One `runtests.jl` that only calls the runner, item files grouped by component, and a `test/Project.toml` for test-only dependencies:

```text
test/
  Project.toml          # Test, TestItemRunner, OffsetArrays, ...
  runtests.jl           # using TestItemRunner; @run_package_tests
  parsing_tests.jl      # @testitem blocks
  solver_tests.jl
  setup.jl              # @testsnippet / @testmodule definitions
```

Item ids contain the file path and the item name, so group by component and name items descriptively (`"parse: rejects trailing garbage"`). There is no `include` list to keep in sync, and no `test/Manifest.toml` is committed.
I have a hundred small `@testitem`s, and each starts with the same five lines of setup. What is the cleanest way to cut the repetition?

Move the setup into a `@testsnippet` and list it in `setup=[...]`:

```julia
# partial
@testsnippet Fixtures begin
    using LinearAlgebra
    A = [4.0 1.0; 1.0 3.0]
    b = [1.0, 2.0]
end

@testitem "solve" setup=[Fixtures] begin
    @test A * (A \ b) ≈ b
end
```

The snippet's code is evaluated again inside every item that lists it, so keep fixtures cheap; I counted three evaluations for three items. Expensive shared setup belongs in a `@testmodule`, whose body I saw evaluated once for three items in the same process.
How can I tell whether the speedup from a warm test worker is real?

Time the same single item both ways, after a warm-up: once through `julia_run_testitems` on a reused worker (run it twice and use the second result), and once through a cold `Pkg.test()` with a filter. The first call into a fresh worker or process pays compilation, so a cold first call is not a measurement of the code. The warm run skips process startup and package load; the cold run also pays Pkg's environment setup. Report the ratio you measured, not a remembered one.
Should my benchmark scripts live in the test suite?

No. Timing assertions in tests fail on a loaded machine, and benchmark dependencies slow down every test environment. Keep benchmarks in a separate `benchmark/` environment and keep tests about correctness. If you want a regression guard, test properties that do not depend on the machine, such as "this call does not allocate" or "this call is type stable" with `@inferred`, rather than absolute times. Before taking any timing, free the machine of idle test workers with `julia_list_test_processes` and `julia_terminate_test_process`.
How do I stop worker leftovers from skewing my benchmarks?

Inventory first. List workers with `julia_list_test_processes`, terminate the ones you do not need with `julia_terminate_test_process`, and check for runs left in a running state (cancel those with `julia_cancel_testrun`). Idle workers hold memory and a stranded run can leave a pool behind, so two identical benchmark runs can differ by a large factor purely because of machine state. If a result looks implausible, suspect the machine before the code.
A subagent I dispatched said "waiting for the long test run to finish" and returned nothing. What went wrong?

It backgrounded the long command and ended its turn. In a subagent the completion notification does not come back to the subagent, so it waits forever and reports no status, even if the work on disk is correct and uncommitted. Run long commands in the foreground with a generous timeout, or use `julia_run_testitems`, which waits up to `max_wait_seconds` and then returns `status: "running"` with a `testrun_id` you can poll with `julia_get_testrun_results` in the same turn. Check `git status` before redoing the work.
Does `Pkg.test()` run my test items in parallel?

By default `@run_package_tests` runs them one after another in the single test process. The parallel workers belong to the agent/editor tooling (`julia_run_testitems` with `max_workers`). When wall-clock time on a full suite matters, use the tool with `max_workers` of 2 to 4 for the inner loop, and keep `Pkg.test()` as the serial, deterministic gate.
Items pass in `julia_run_testitems` but fail under `Pkg.test()`. Why would that be?

The environments and flags differ. Likely causes, in order:

1. Bounds checking: on Julia 1.10-1.12 `Pkg.test()` forces `--check-bounds=yes`, so an out-of-range access inside `@inbounds` code raises `BoundsError` there and passes silently in a warm worker.
2. A stale warm worker: it holds old definitions or leftover state. A cold `Pkg.test()` is the reference.
3. A test dependency missing from `test/Project.toml` that happens to be loadable in the worker's environment.
4. `runtests.jl` applies a `filter` that the tool does not, or the reverse.

Reproduce in the failing mode: `Pkg.test(; test_args=...)` or print `Base.JLOptions().check_bounds` first, and fix the code, not the mode.
Items pass under `Pkg.test()` on 1.13 but CI on 1.10 fails with `BoundsError`. We never saw it locally.

Consistent with the version difference. On 1.10 through 1.12, `Pkg.test()` runs the tests with `--check-bounds=yes`; on 1.13 it inherits the session's setting, so a default 1.13 run executes `@inbounds` code with its checks removed and the bug stays silent. I confirmed both: on 1.13.2 `Pkg.test()` reported `check_bounds = 0` and an `@inbounds` read of an empty vector returned a value without error, while on 1.10 and 1.12 it raised `BoundsError`. Reproduce locally with `Pkg.test(; julia_args=["--check-bounds=yes"])`, then fix the `@inbounds` code (or the indexing it relies on) rather than excluding that version.
I just fixed a bug in `parse_header` in `src/parser.jl`. How should I verify it?

Run the parser's items, not the whole suite:

```text
1. julia_list_testitems       name_pattern="parse"           # get the ids
2. julia_run_testitems        name_pattern="parse"  max_workers=1
3. julia_get_testitem_detail  testrun_id=<id>  testitem_ids=[<failed ids>]   # only on failure
```

If the bug had no failing test, add one and confirm it fails against the old code before you rely on it. Run the full suite only if `parse_header` is shared by other components, as a gate before the commit.
The fix works. Can I commit?

Check the gate first. In order:

1. The filtered items for the changed component pass.
2. A regression test exists and was seen to fail without the fix.
3. If the change touched shared code: the full suite passes, as a cold `Pkg.test()` from the package root, and once per Julia version in the CI matrix.
4. Leftover test workers are reaped (`julia_list_test_processes`, then `julia_terminate_test_process` per id).

Then commit, and say in the message which behavior the change establishes. Do not cite the plan or session that led to it.
Run the whole suite, please, just to be safe.

I would rather scope it. A full run on every iteration is slow and hides which change caused a failure. If the edit is confined to one component, run its items:

```text
julia_run_testitems  file_pattern="parser"  max_workers=1
```

and run the full suite once, as the pre-commit gate, if the change touches shared code (a planner, shared kernels, routing). If you want the full suite now, I will run it with `max_workers=2` and a per-item `timeout`, then reap the workers afterward.
The agent ran `Pkg.test()` after every small edit and each run took minutes. How do I fix the workflow?

Split inner loop and gate. Inner loop: `julia_run_testitems` with `items` or `name_pattern` and `max_workers=1`, on a warm worker that reloads edits through Revise. Gate: one cold `Pkg.test()` before the commit. On Julia 1.10-1.12 each `Pkg.test()` also runs under a forced `--check-bounds=yes` and compiles the package a second time under that flag, which is one reason it is slow after every source change (on 1.13 Pkg inherits the session's flag, so that extra compile appears only if you pass it). If a failing test needs a repro in the `Pkg.test` environment, on 1.10-1.12 use `Pkg.test(; julia_args=["--check-bounds=auto"])` to iterate, and drop the override for the real gate.
I want to add a feature with tests first. How do I use the tools for that?

1. Write the `@testitem` (name it descriptively; tag it if it is slow).
2. `julia_list_testitems` with `name_pattern` to confirm the item is detected; if it is missing, `julia_get_diagnostics` on the file shows item-declaration errors.
3. `julia_run_testitems` for the item and confirm it fails for the expected reason: read `julia_get_testitem_detail`, since a failure from a typo proves nothing.
4. Implement.
5. `julia_rerun_failed` with the earlier `testrun_id` until green.
6. Run the related items, then the gate as needed.

Step 3 matters: a test you never saw fail may be vacuous.
Please run the tests for me and tell me whether my change is okay.

I will run them with a bounded pool and report the scope with the result:

```text
julia_set_workspace_folders   folders=[<package root>]
julia_run_testitems           max_workers=2  timeout=300
```

I will report the number of items run, how many passed, and for any failure the message from `julia_get_testitem_detail`, plus which Julia version ran them. If you need results on another version, I will repeat the run with `julia_cmd` for it. A bare "tests pass" would not say which items or versions that covers.
I ran `julia_run_testitems` and it says 1 errored, 0 failed, and the item body is just two `@test`s. What does "errored" mean here?

"Failed" means an assertion evaluated to false. "Errored" means an exception escaped, or the item could not run at all: a timeout, an unhandled error in the body, a failure to activate the environment, or a worker that died. Look at `julia_get_testitem_detail`: the first message names the cause. If it mentions environment activation or the worker, the assertions never ran, so fix `test/Project.toml` or the load error (the raw output is in `testprocess://{process_id}/output`) before touching the test code.
Is `Pkg.test()` faster than the MCP test tool since it is the "official" runner?

No, it is slower for repeated runs. `Pkg.test()` starts a new process, builds a temporary environment, and recompiles, whereas `julia_run_testitems` reuses worker processes that keep compiled code and apply your edits with Revise. Use the tool for iteration. `Pkg.test()` is the right choice as the final gate precisely because it is cold: nothing in it depends on warm state.
Since Revise reloads my edits in the worker, I can skip the cold `Pkg.test()` before committing, right?

No. A long-lived worker can hide stale definitions, leftover global state, and world-age problems that a fresh process exposes, and it does not run with the `Pkg.test()` environment and flags. Revise makes iteration fast; the cold gate checks that the code on disk works from a clean start. Run it once before a commit or merge.
`max_workers=1` seems slow for the full suite. Is it okay to raise it?

Yes. `max_workers=1` is for iteration on one item or a handful. For a full suite where wall-clock time matters, use 2 to 4, and leave cores free for other work. What to avoid is the default (CPU threads, capped at 8 and at one per 3 GiB of memory), because each worker loads your package and its dependencies. Reap workers after the run.
My test uses random numbers and sometimes fails in CI. How do I make it reliable?

Seed an explicit RNG and assert properties instead of stored values:

```julia
using Random, Test

rng = Xoshiro(1234)
x = rand(rng, 1000)
@test all(0 .<= x .< 1)
@test abs(sum(x) / length(x) - 0.5) < 0.05
```

Do not compare against numbers recorded from `rand` on another Julia version. The documentation of `Random.default_rng` states that across versions you should not expect the default RNG to produce the same stream for a given seed. If you need an identical stream everywhere, use a package that guarantees it (such as StableRNGs) or generate the data deterministically without randomness.

Review this test for flakiness.

```julia
using Test
@testset "timing" begin
    t = @elapsed sleep(0.1)
    @test t < 0.11
end
```

It asserts an upper bound on wall-clock time, which depends on machine load, the scheduler, and `sleep` granularity, so it fails intermittently on a busy CI runner. Test what the code does, not how long it took: assert the lower bound, which `sleep` guarantees, or inject a clock.

```julia
using Test
@testset "timing" begin
    t = @elapsed sleep(0.1)
    @test t >= 0.1
end
```

If performance is the requirement, measure it with a benchmark in a separate environment and compare ratios, not with an absolute-time assertion in the unit tests.

Review this `runtests.jl`. Why is it a maintenance burden?

```julia
# partial
using Test, MyPkg
include("parsing_tests.jl")
include("solver_tests.jl")
include("io_tests.jl")
```

Every new test file has to be added by hand, and everything shares one module and one process, so a test can depend on a name defined by an earlier file and nothing detects it. Test items remove both problems:

```julia
# partial
using TestItemRunner
@run_package_tests
```

Convert each `@testset` block to a `@testitem "..." begin ... end` that has its own imports or setup, put `TestItemRunner` in `test/Project.toml`, and delete the `include` list. Items are found by parsing, run in isolation, and can be filtered or rerun individually.

Convert this to a test item.

```julia
# partial
@testset "norm" begin
    v = [3.0, 4.0]
    @test norm(v) == 5.0
end
```

The `norm` function comes from `LinearAlgebra`, so the item must import it itself, since items do not inherit imports from `runtests.jl`:

```julia
# partial
@testitem "norm of a 3-4 vector" begin
    using LinearAlgebra
    v = [3.0, 4.0]
    @test norm(v) == 5.0
end
```

`Test` and your package are already imported by default. `@testset` is optional: the item is already a test set, and the name becomes the item's id. If many items share `using LinearAlgebra`, put it in a `@testsnippet` and list it in `setup=[...]`.
Is it a problem if my test items print a lot of output?

Output of a passing item is captured and only shown through `julia_get_testitem_detail`, so the run summary stays readable. But very large output (profiles, task dumps, big arrays) bloats the stored detail; the tool keeps only the tail by default. Print less in items, and when you need output, ask for `julia_get_testitem_detail` with `max_output_bytes` set to what you want to read.
A passing test run took 0.2 seconds but a cold `Pkg.test()` took 20 seconds. Is the warm number a fair benchmark of my code?

It measures iteration latency, not the code. The warm figure leaves out process start, package load, and compilation, which a warm worker has already paid. Julia's first call of a method compiles it, so any timing from a cold process is mostly compile time. If you want to know how fast the code runs, benchmark it with BenchmarkTools after a warm-up call, using the median. If you want to know why the gate is slow, look at precompilation (on 1.10-1.12 a second one under `--check-bounds=yes`).
Do I need `Pkg.precompile()` before running the tests?

It helps with a heavy dependency stack. The first load of a package with large dependencies can take minutes, and that cost lands on whichever command runs first, which can make a tool call time out and look like a failure. Run `julia --project=<path> -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.precompile()'` once in the foreground, then start the tests. For `julia_run_testitems`, raise `max_wait_seconds` for the first run if needed; the call returns as soon as the run finishes, so a larger value costs nothing.
Can a test environment have a different set of package versions than the main project?

Yes, within the compat bounds. `Pkg.test()` merges the package's `Project.toml` with `test/Project.toml` and resolves them together, so a test dependency that conflicts with the package's compat bounds produces a resolver error. Resolve conflicts by adjusting `[compat]` in `test/Project.toml` or the package, and run `Pkg.resolve()` on the package project; do not create a `test/Manifest.toml` to force versions.
I've created a `test/Manifest.toml` by accident while adding a test dependency. What do I do?

Delete it and make sure it is ignored:

```text
rm test/Manifest.toml
echo "test/Manifest.toml" >> .gitignore
```

The dependency itself lives in `test/Project.toml` and is enough: `Pkg.test()` resolves a temporary environment from it every run, and the test-item tooling builds its own sandbox from it. Avoid running `Pkg.resolve()` or `Pkg.instantiate()` with `--project=test` in the future, since those write the manifest.
Should I test internal helper functions or only the public API?

Test the public API thoroughly, since it is the contract. Test internals only where a bug would be hard to see through the public interface (an indexing helper, a parser state machine), and keep those tests easy to delete when the implementation changes. Tests that pin down incidental structure make refactors expensive and rarely catch a bug the public tests would not.
Our `@testitem` for an `AbstractMatrix` function only uses `rand(5, 5)`. Is that enough?
I wrote `@test f(x) == y` where `f` should throw for bad input, and I have no negative tests at all. Is that okay?

Add them. A suite with only happy-path assertions cannot tell whether a function rejects bad input or silently returns a wrong value. For each documented precondition add a `@test_throws` with the message (see the `@test_throws "message" expr` form), and for each helper with a gating condition add an input that must make it fail. Negative tests are what keep validation from being deleted in a later refactor.
What does a good test item name look like?

A short statement of the behavior, because the name is the item's identity: it appears in the id (`MyPkg@a1b2c3d4/test/parsing_tests.jl::parse: rejects trailing garbage`), in failure reports, and in `name_pattern` filters. Prefer `"parse: rejects trailing garbage"` over `"test 3"`. Keep names unique within a file, since the id is built from the file and the name. Rename an item only when you also expect saved ids to become invalid.
How do I test code that uses multiple threads?

Start the worker with threads and test for the property that must hold, not for scheduling. For the agent tool, `julia_run_testitems` takes `julia_num_threads` (for example `"4"`); in `Pkg.test()` pass `julia_args=["--threads=4"]`. Compare the threaded result with a serial reference (`@test threaded_f(x) ≈ serial_f(x)`), and run it a few times to expose races. Do not assert timing or the number of tasks that ran.
I changed `test/Project.toml` and the existing workers still behave as before. Is the environment stale?

The idle workers were started with the old environment. To get a fresh one, terminate them with `julia_list_test_processes` and `julia_terminate_test_process`, then rerun; the replacement worker starts from the current `test/Project.toml`. Check that the edit is correct first: a bad dependency line makes every item error with an environment activation message.
Is there any reason to keep a test item's expected values in a file?

Yes, for large golden data: store a reference in a data file next to the tests and load it inside the item. But the comparison helper becomes part of the test, so give it a negative control (two inputs that must compare unequal), and avoid recording values that vary across Julia versions, such as hashes, default-RNG output, or `objectid`. Record the inputs and the property, or use a version-independent reference.
Do `@testitem`s work with code coverage?

Yes. Run `julia_run_testitems` with `mode="Coverage"` and read the lines with `julia_get_coverage_results`. Coverage collection is for the packages under test. Treat the percentage as a pointer to untested branches, not as proof of correctness: a covered line with a vacuous assertion still passes.
Three items failed after my change. What do I do first?
Get the messages, batched into one call: `julia_get_testitem_detail` with the `testrun_id` and all three ids. Read the first message of each before editing anything.
Two say `BoundsError` at an index of 0, and the third says `UndefVarError: cache`.

Two separate causes. The `BoundsError` at index 0 points to an indexing assumption: look for `1:length(A)` or an offset that is off by one, and prefer `eachindex(A)`. The `UndefVarError` in an item usually means the item relied on a global defined by another item; items run in separate modules, so move the definition into a `@testsnippet` listed in `setup=[...]`. Fix both, then call `julia_rerun_failed` with the earlier `testrun_id`, which reruns only these three on the warm workers.
My CI is green on Julia 1.13 but red on 1.10. I only have 1.13 locally.
Install the LTS (`juliaup add 1.10`) and reproduce there before changing code. From the agent tools, call `julia_run_testitems` with `julia_cmd` set to the 1.10 `julia` binary and `max_workers=1`.
On 1.10 an item fails with a `BoundsError` inside an `@inbounds` loop.

That fits the version difference: on 1.10 `Pkg.test()` forces `--check-bounds=yes`, which neutralizes `@inbounds` and exposes the bad index, while a default 1.13 `Pkg.test()` inherits the session setting and hides it. Fix the indexing (iterate `eachindex`, or establish the in-bounds property and cover it with a test). Then on 1.13 run `Pkg.test(; julia_args=["--check-bounds=yes"])` so local runs match CI.
